topicName: Distributed Training (Data Parallelism, Tensor Parallelism, Pipeline Parallelism)
content:
[{"order":1,"type":"heading","text":"Distributed Training Strategies: Data, Tensor, and Pipeline Parallelism"},{"order":2,"type":"paragraph","text":"As deep learning models grow to hundreds of billions or trillions of parameters, fitting them into the memory of a single GPU becomes impossible. Distributed training solves this limitation by splitting the computational workload and model parameters across multiple GPUs and nodes. This tutorial covers the three fundamental pillars of distributed training: Data Parallelism, Tensor Parallelism, and Pipeline Parallelism."},{"order":3,"type":"subheading","text":"1. Data Parallelism (DP)"},{"order":4,"type":"paragraph","text":"Data Parallelism is the most common and straightforward scaling technique. In this approach, a full copy of the model is loaded onto every available GPU. The global dataset is split into smaller mini-batches, and each GPU processes a distinct mini-batch independently. After the forward and backward passes, GPUs must synchronize their gradients to update the model weights uniformly."},{"order":5,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Standard Data Parallelism (DP): Replicates the model and uses a parameter server or central GPU to average gradients, which often creates communication bottlenecks."},{"order":6,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Distributed Data Parallel (DDP): Utilizes ring-allreduce communication algorithms to overlap computation with gradient synchronization, significantly scaling better across multiple nodes."},{"order":7,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Fully Sharded Data Parallel (FSDP): Shards optimizer states, gradients, and model parameters across GPUs, dramatically reducing memory overhead compared to standard DDP."},{"order":8,"type":"code","text":"import torch
import torch.distributed as dist
from torch.nn.parallel import DistributedDataParallel as DDP

# Initialize process group
dist.init_process_group(backend="nccl")
local_rank = dist.get_rank()
torch.cuda.set_device(local_rank)

# Create model and wrap with DDP
model = MyDeepLearningModel().to(local_rank)
model = DDP(model, device_ids=[local_rank])

optimizer = torch.optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=1e-3)"},{"order":9,"type":"subheading","text":"2. Tensor Parallelism (TP)"},{"order":10,"type":"paragraph","text":"When a single model layer is too large to fit into GPU memory, Tensor Parallelism (also known as intra-layer parallelism) splits individual weight matrices across multiple devices. This is frequently used for massive Multi-Head Attention (MHA) and Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) blocks in Transformer architectures like Megatron-LM."},{"order":11,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Column-Parallel Linear Layers: The weight matrix W is split column-wise across GPUs. Each GPU computes a portion of the output features, followed by an all-reduce or concatenation step."},{"order":12,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Row-Parallel Linear Layers: The weight matrix W is split row-wise across GPUs. The outputs from each GPU are summed up using an all-reduce operation."},{"order":13,"type":"code","text":"# Conceptual example of splitting a linear layer for Tensor Parallelism
class ColumnParallelLinear(torch.nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, in_features, out_features):
        super().__init__()
        # Split output features across world size
        world_size = dist.get_world_size()
        self.out_features_per_partition = out_features // world_size
        self.weight = torch.nn.Parameter(torch.randn(self.out_features_per_partition, in_features))

    def forward(self, x):
        return torch.matmul(x, self.weight.t())"},{"order":14,"type":"subheading","text":"3. Pipeline Parallelism (PP)"},{"order":15,"type":"paragraph","text":"Pipeline Parallelism (inter-layer parallelism) divides a deep model sequentially by placing different layers on different GPUs. For example, layers 1-8 reside on GPU 0, layers 9-16 on GPU 1, and so on. Because GPU 2 must wait for GPU 1 to finish its forward pass, naive pipeline parallelism leads to massive GPU idle time (pipeline bubbles)."},{"order":16,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Micro-batching: To reduce bubbles, the input mini-batch is split into smaller micro-batches that flow through the pipeline sequentially."},{"order":17,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Schedule Types: Advanced scheduling algorithms like GPipe and 1F1B (One Forward, One Backward) interleave forward and backward passes to maximize GPU utilization and minimize memory footprints."},{"order":18,"type":"code","text":"# Using PyTorch RPC or specialized libraries like DeepSpeed / Megatron for Pipeline Parallelism
from torch.distributed.pipeline.sync import Pipe

# Sequential model split into stages
net = torch.nn.Sequential(
    LayerStage1().to(0),
    LayerStage2().to(1)
)

# Wrap in Pipe with micro-batching
batch_size = 32
chunks = 4
pipelined_model = Pipe(net, chunks=chunks)"},{"order":19,"type":"subheading","text":"Conclusion and 3D Parallelism"},{"order":20,"type":"paragraph","text":"Modern large language model (LLM) training rarely relies on just one strategy. Instead, production frameworks combine Data Parallelism, Tensor Parallelism, and Pipeline Parallelism simultaneously—a paradigm known as 3D Parallelism. By properly aligning these strategies with the underlying hardware interconnects (like NVLink and InfiniBand), developers can efficiently train models with hundreds of billions of parameters."}]
